idea.why: An orchestrator that owns sorting and presentation plus one specialist per data domain, each with a narrow job and explicit anti-hallucination and empty-section rules. The conceptual gap is that document rendering is treated as a prompt instruction rather than a concern of its own, so layout correctness rides entirely on model compliance.

structure.why: Idiomatic types for every job, with sub-agents exposed as callable tools and native filters used instead of post-filtering downstream. Eight nodes is proportionate with no merge or set ceremony. Quibble: no template node, so the deliverable is unvalidated model text.

connections.why: One model fans out to all three agents, and each data tool attaches to the agent that needs it rather than being dumped on the orchestrator. The main chain contains only genuinely dependent steps; the two independent fetches hang off separate sub-agents rather than being serialised.

answer.why: End to end it does what was asked and the author would recognise their request. Two shortfalls: the HTML passes straight through with no guard, so a stray fence renders as literal text, and the dashboard is delivered as an email rather than anything browsable during the day.

appraisal: The right shape for a multi-agent brief: an orchestrator with two domain specialists, each owning one source and one reasoning job, sharing a single model and wired so nothing independent is needlessly serialised. The tools are used natively, with real time filters and proper day bounds. Its weak point is the deliverable: the entire dashboard is free-form model output piped unvalidated into the mail body, so renderability depends on the model never emitting a fence or a line of commentary. A knowledgeable user would force structured output and render from a fixed template, or at minimum insert a fence-stripping step before the send.
